**Solution 3 has the correct final answer, 6.** I checked it by hand, not against the source paper, so the n = 6 and n ≥ 7 parts are partly heuristic.

**n = 4 fails.** A single 4-edge covers all triples, but Berge-C₄³ needs 4 distinct edges.

**n = 5 fails.** Take H = {V∖{i} : i = 1,…,4} on V = {1,…,5}. A triple T is uncovered only if every missing index lies in T, which needs 4 elements in a 3-set, so δ₃ ≥ 1. H has only 4 edges, so it has no Berge-C₅³. Solution 3's specific construction (three 4-sets covering all 10 triples) is impossible, since the three missing-vertex triples would be uncovered. Its conclusion for n = 5 is still right.

**n = 6 appears to hold.** Any counterexample can be reduced to a minimal cover, since extra edges only help.
- A cover with ≤ 5 edges is impossible: 4-edges cover at most 4 triples each, and a counting argument on the complement graph rules out every mix with ≤ 5 edges.
- The only 6-edge cover is the six 4-sets whose complementary pairs form two disjoint triangles. I found a cyclic arrangement giving a Berge-C₆³, and a Berge-C₄³ and C₅³ also exist.
- I checked two further minimal 7- and 8-edge covers (the K₂∪K₄ complement and an 8-edge maximal triangle-free complement). Each yields a Berge-C₆³. I did not exhaust all mixed 3-edge/4-edge covers with more edges.

**n ≥ 7** has no edge-count obstruction, since a cover needs at least C(n,3)/4 > n edges. I did not verify all structures there. Solution 1's claim that n = 6 fails rests on an unsupported construction, and Solution 2's final answer of 3 is contradicted by the n = 4 and n = 5 counterexamples.

CHOICE: 3
